title: Canadian river ice-flag seasons became 0.6 days shorter, not the 3.3 days that air-temperature sensitivity predicts, at 568 HYDAT stations from 1966-1995 to 1996-2025; the gap is in western rivers
abstract:
Question: Water Survey of Canada stations flag ice-affected daily discharge with the symbol B. Does the year-to-year sensitivity of the first and last B day to local air temperature, fitted in 1966-1995, predict the mean change in 1996-2025?

Method: We used the HYDAT release of 2026-10-19 and GHCN-CAMS monthly air temperature. We kept 568 stations with complete 1 September to 31 July records, persistent ice and at least 15 winters in each period. A pooled within-station regression gave the sensitivity of each date to a two-month temperature window. We compared observed and predicted station-mean shifts, with 95% intervals from a bootstrap over HYDAT sub-drainage areas.

Results: The cold-season air warmed by 0.8-1.0 C. The model predicted a 3.3-day [2.9, 3.7] shorter ice-flag season. The observed season became 0.6 days shorter (95% interval: 2.5 days shorter to 1.6 days longer). The first B day did not become later (observed +0.1 d, predicted +2.5 d). The break-up proxy agreed with the prediction within its interval. The gap is regional: Ontario, the Maritimes and Manitoba followed the prediction, but in British Columbia and Alberta the flagged season became 4.4 days longer [2.3, 6.4], and the North and Newfoundland and Labrador also had positive gaps. More sporadic short B runs explain part of the national gap: with runs of 14 or more consecutive B days, the gap on the same 449 stations fell from +2.2 d [0.4, 4.1] to +0.9 d [-1.2, 3.1], but the western and northern gaps stayed (West +2.8 d, North +4.9 d). In a 1981-2002 to 2003-2025 test, the season did not shorten (gap +4.2 d flag dates, +2.8 d continuous runs). Pre-freeze-up discharge did not explain the gap. Results were similar with Berkeley Earth temperature and another split year.

Limitations: The B flag is an indirect ice indicator that depends on hydrometric practice; regional offices follow geography, so we cannot separate a practice change from a physical change. Window means do not show snow or cold snaps. The sample favours long-running southern stations.

display.caption: Change in ice-flag season length from 1966-1995 to 1996-2025 by region: observed (blue circles) and predicted from 1966-1995 air-temperature sensitivity (orange squares), with 95% sub-drainage bootstrap intervals. Left: first to last B-flag day. Right: first to last run of 14 or more consecutive B days. Eastern regions follow the prediction; western, northern and Newfoundland rivers do not.

National mean station anomalies (blue) of the first B day, last B day and B-season length, and the anomalies predicted by the pooled 1966-1995 temperature sensitivity (orange), 1966-2025. Dashed lines are period means. Grey band: training period.

Left and centre: the number of separate B-flag runs per winter and the days of sporadic flags at the season edges increased. Right: observed minus predicted shift on the same 449 stations for flag dates (blue) and 14-day-run dates (orange); the run definition removes most of the national gap.

citations.reason: Defines first and last B dates as freeze-up and break-up proxies and documents their caveats.
Reported earlier freeze-up in Canadian rivers from RHBN data; we test whether B dates follow air temperature over decades.
Recent analysis of ice-influenced maximum water levels from the Canadian River Ice Database.
Same test design for lake ice; lake ice-on became later than air-temperature models predicted, while river first-B dates became earlier.
GHCN-CAMS gridded land air temperature used as the main temperature input.
